claims.claim: Pierson v. Post (N.Y. 1805): mere pursuit gives no property right; capture or mortal wounding required; dissent favored hunters' custom and killing noxious foxes
claims.note: N.Y. Supreme Court of Judicature, 1805.

claims.claim: Ghen v. Rich (D. Mass. 1881): whale killed by bomb lance washed ashore; court enforced whalers' custom for the killer
claims.note: Finder (Ellis) sold to Rich; lesson's 'stranger took it and sold the oil' is a slight compression.

claims.claim: Rule of capture: driller owns oil/gas/groundwater drained from beneath a neighbor's land; conservation/spacing regulation softened it
Elements: actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile, continuous for the statutory period; government land generally immune
Statutory period commonly about five to twenty or more years by state
claims.note: Source gives a US range of 5 to 40 years; 'twenty or more' is consistent.

claims.claim: Howard v. Kunto (Wash. 1970) allowed tacking where deeds did not describe the occupied land
claims.note: Court was the Washington Court of Appeals (3 Wn. App. 393), so the citation should read Wash. Ct. App. 1970.

claims.claim: Gruen v. Gruen (N.Y. 1986): letter gave present gift of a remainder in a painting with retained life estate; physical delivery not required
claims.note: Opinion also states the three gift elements: intent, delivery (actual or constructive), acceptance.

claims.claim: Armory v. Delamirie (K.B. 1722): chimney sweep's boy's jewel; apprentice removed stones; finder's title good against all but true owner
Hannah v. Peel (K.B. 1945): soldier finder of brooch prevailed over house owner who never occupied it or knew of the brooch
Fee simple determinable uses durational words, ends automatically, grantor holds possibility of reverter
Fee simple subject to condition subsequent uses 'but if' and does not end automatically; grantor must act
Most states abolished the fee tail
claims.note: Source: abolished in all but four U.S. states.

claims.claim: Contingent remainder = created in unascertained person or subject to condition precedent
Executory interest either shifts (divests another transferee) or springs (divests the grantor)
Worked example: 'to A for life, then to B if B survives A' gives B an ALTERNATIVE contingent remainder
claims.note: An alternative contingent remainder needs two alternative takers; here B has a plain contingent remainder and O a reversion (the lesson's own reversion analysis shows it is not alternative).

claims.claim: Gray's classic formulation (must vest, if at all, within 21 years after a life in being); origin in Duke of Norfolk's Case (1682)
USRAP (1986) validates interests that vest within 90 years; some jurisdictions abolished the rule, allowing dynasty trusts
claims.note: Source: 29 states/territories adopted USRAP or a variant; at least six states repealed the rule entirely; others extend to 360/1000 years (e.g., Florida).

claims.claim: Unborn widow: 'a gift to the widow's children is void'
claims.note: Mis-stated: the classic void gift is to the life tenant's (son's) children living at the widow's death, not to 'the widow's children'. Question l06.q4 states it correctly.

claims.claim: Four unities of joint tenancy: time, title, interest, possession; tenancy by the entirety shields property from creditors of one spouse
claims.note: LII says tenancy by the entirety is recognized in 'most states'; lesson says 'some states' (minor).

claims.claim: In lien theory states a mortgage by one joint tenant does not sever and the lien fails if the borrower dies first (Harms v. Sprague, Ill. 1984)
claims.note: Harms v. Sprague: Illinois Supreme Court, Nov. 30, 1984.
